transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

I guess I’m here because things have gotten… bigger than I can keep up with. I’m an artist, so I’m used to juggling projects, but lately I’ve been saying yes to everything — new pieces, workshops, changing things around in the studio, taking client calls at all hours, planning improvements I probably should have waited on. At first it felt productive, like I was finally getting momentum, but now I look at the list and it’s just too much.

The deadlines are starting to pile up, and there’s money pressure too — the mortgage especially is sitting in the back of my mind. I keep thinking I can make it all work if I just push harder, but realistically I’ve taken on more than one person can manage. So… I thought I should come in before it gets completely out of hand.
Have you been feeling anxious about not meeting these deadlines or managing your workload?

Yes… anxious is probably the right word, though it feels more like this constant pressure, like everything is stacked up behind me and I’m trying to keep it from falling over. I came in because I’ve taken on way more than I can realistically manage — projects, workshops, studio changes I thought would “improve the flow,” client calls at odd hours, all of it.

At the time each thing felt important, and honestly manageable if I just organized it correctly, but now the deadlines are closing in and I’m realizing I may have stretched myself too far. And then the mortgage is there in the background, so it’s not just creative stress — it feels like if I don’t keep everything moving, something important could slip. So yes, I’m worried about not meeting the deadlines, but also about the whole workload getting away from me.
Do you find yourself having repetitive thoughts that you can't seem to stop thinking about?

I’m not sure I’d call them repetitive thoughts exactly. I mean, I do go over things in my head — the schedule, what I promised people, whether I’ve forgotten some detail — but it feels more like trying to keep track of too many moving pieces than one particular thought looping in a way I can’t stop.

If you mean like… the same phrase or fear coming back over and over no matter what I do, I don’t think I’ve noticed that. It’s more that my mind keeps returning to the whole pile of responsibilities because there are so many of them, and I’m worried I’ll miss something important.
Have you been avoiding certain tasks or situations because of feeling overwhelmed?

I’m not sure I’d say I’m avoiding things in a deliberate way. It’s more… I’ll look at the list and some parts of it feel so tangled that I don’t know where to start, so I end up doing something nearby instead — reorganizing supplies, answering a less important email, checking the calendar again — things that still feel like work, but maybe aren’t the thing that actually needs doing.

But I don’t know if that counts as avoidance or just being overloaded. I haven’t really been saying, “I can’t face this, so I won’t do it.” It’s more like I circle around the harder tasks because there are so many steps and I’m trying to find the right entry point. Then suddenly an hour has gone by and I’ve handled ten little things, but not the main thing I meant to start.
Do you feel compelled to perform specific rituals or behaviors to reduce your anxiety?

I don’t think so, no… not in the way I think you mean. I don’t have, like, a set thing I have to do a certain number of times or a ritual I believe will make the anxiety go away.

I do sometimes rearrange things in the studio or make lists and then rewrite the lists, but that feels more like trying to get a handle on the chaos than a compulsion. Like if the brushes are in the right place or the schedule is clearer, maybe I can breathe a little and see what needs to happen next. But I’m not thinking, “If I don’t do this exact thing, something terrible will happen.” It’s more practical, or at least it seems practical at the time.

So… I guess I’d say I use organizing to calm myself down, but I haven’t noticed any specific rituals that I feel forced to do.
Is the feeling of pressure and anxiety you've described limited to your work and deadlines, or does it also affect other areas of your life?

It’s not just work, unfortunately. I mean, work is where it shows up most visibly because there are deadlines and other people can see when something slips. My illustration deadlines have slipped more than once, and a couple of colleagues have had to check in with me, not in an accusatory way exactly, but more like, “Are you still on track?” or “Do you need help figuring out the next step?” And that feels awful, because I’m used to being the person who can handle a lot.

But it’s spilled over beyond that. The bigger thing — and I’m embarrassed to say this — is that I overcommitted. I said yes to too many projects, too many plans, too many purchases for the studio, thinking I could make it all work if I just pushed harder. And I spent money that I really needed to keep the studio secure. So now the mortgage is at risk, which is… that’s not just a work deadline problem. That’s my home, my stability, everything.

So yes, the pressure started around work and deadlines, or at least that’s where I noticed it first, but it’s affecting the rest of my life now. It’s gotten into finances and housing and my relationships with colleagues who are having to watch me more closely than they should have to.
Are you finding it difficult to enjoy time with friends and family or engage in activities you normally like to do because of the pressure and anxiety you're feeling?

I don’t know if I’d put it that strongly. I haven’t noticed myself completely pulling away from people or not liking things I usually like. It’s more that when I’m with someone, part of my mind is still sort of… hovering over the unfinished things. So I might be sitting with a friend or talking to family, and I’m trying to be present, but there’s this background noise of, “You should be handling that other thing.”

But I wouldn’t say I can’t enjoy them at all. If someone gets me out of my own head a little, I can still laugh, I can still get absorbed in a conversation, and I still like being around people I care about. Same with activities — I can still appreciate them once I’m actually there. It’s just harder to settle into them because the pressure keeps tugging at me.

So… maybe it interferes some, but I haven’t really been avoiding friends or family because of it, at least not in a clear way that I’ve noticed.
Is there anything in particular that you worry about when you're not thinking about work or deadlines?

Yes… there is one thing, and I know it’s going to sound a little extreme when I say it out loud. It wasn’t exactly a normal “I’m worried they won’t like my work” kind of worry. I became really certain that a couple of clients — and even one editor I’ve worked with — were trying to get access to my sketches before I unveiled the whole system I’d been developing.

I kept thinking they were asking for updates or files in a way that wasn’t just about the project. Like there was some other motive underneath it. And people tried to reassure me, they’d say, “No, we’re just checking in,” or “We need this for scheduling,” things like that, but it didn’t really settle me. I would hear it and understand what they were saying, but the certainty didn’t go away.

It’s uncomfortable to admit because part of me can hear how suspicious it sounds. But at the time it felt very real, like I had to protect the sketches until I was ready to reveal everything properly.
Do you find yourself having thoughts that you consider unreasonable or irrational, but that you cannot stop thinking about?

Yes… though I keep hesitating over the word “irrational,” because at the time it didn’t feel irrational. It felt like I was seeing something other people weren’t taking seriously enough.

The main thing was with my sketches. I became really convinced that a couple of clients, and even an editor I’ve worked with, were trying to get access to them before I was ready to unveil the larger system I’d been developing. Like when they asked for updates or wanted files, I didn’t hear it as just normal project management. I kept thinking, “No, they’re trying to get the framework before it’s complete,” or “They want to see the underlying structure so they can use it before I present it properly.”

And people did reassure me. They would say, “We’re not trying to take anything, we just need to see where the work is,” or “This is just for scheduling.” But it didn’t settle in. I could hear the words, and a part of me could understand that maybe it sounded extreme, but the certainty stayed there anyway. It was hard to let go of, even when I tried to talk myself down.
Do you feel like these worries about your clients and editor are thoughts that pop into your head without you wanting them to?

Not exactly like they “pop in” out of nowhere, no. It wasn’t like a random unwanted thought flashing through my mind and then I’d think, “Why am I thinking that?” It felt more… connected to what was happening. Like they would email asking for an update, or someone would mention needing to see the sketches, and then this whole certainty would come over me that they were trying to get access before I was ready to unveil the full system.

I know that probably sounds extreme, and I can hear that. But at the time it didn’t feel like just a nervous thought I could dismiss. It felt solid. I was certain a couple of clients, and even one editor, had some motive beyond what they were saying. And even when they reassured me — like, “No, we just need to see the progress,” or “This is normal scheduling stuff” — it didn’t really calm me down. I heard them, but it didn’t settle the feeling.

So… I wouldn’t say I wanted to be thinking about it, because it was stressful and made everything harder. But it also didn’t feel like some intrusive nonsense thought. It felt real, like I had to protect the sketches until I could reveal everything properly.
Do you still believe that those clients and the editor were trying to get access to your sketches for reasons other than what they stated?

I… yes, mostly. I know sitting here that it sounds extreme, and I can say that out loud now in a way I maybe couldn’t before. But I did become really certain that a couple of clients and even that one editor weren’t just asking for ordinary progress updates. It felt like they were trying to get access to the sketches before I had unveiled the whole system, before I had it arranged and presented the way it needed to be.

And the thing is, people did reassure me. They said it was just scheduling, or they just needed to see where the work stood, or that they weren’t trying to take anything. But it didn’t really land. I heard them, I understood the sentences, but it didn’t settle me. There was still this feeling that there was another reason underneath what they were saying.

So… yes, I still have trouble fully letting go of the idea that there was more to it than they admitted. I know how that sounds. But at the time it felt very real, like I had to protect the sketches until I was ready.
Is the kind of worry you've been experiencing about your work and sketches also something you find happening in other areas of your life, like your relationships or daily routines?

Not really in the same way, no. I mean, I can be sensitive in relationships or get particular about my routines, like anyone, but this was much more focused on the work — the sketches, the system, how and when it was going to be shown.

It wasn’t like I was thinking everyone in my life had hidden motives about everything. It was specifically that a couple of clients, and even one editor, were trying to get access to the sketches before I was ready. And I know that sounds extreme when I say it plainly like that, but at the time it felt very clear to me. Every request for an update felt like it had this other layer underneath it.

They did reassure me, more than once, and said it was just normal progress checking or scheduling, but it didn’t settle me. I kept coming back to the same conclusion — that they wanted to see the structure before I’d unveiled it properly. So, no, I wouldn’t say it’s spread across my whole life in that exact way. It’s been centered around the work and protecting it.
Is the kind of excessive worry you're experiencing about your work something that also happens to you in other areas of your life?

No, not really in other areas the same way. I mean, I worry about ordinary things, of course, but this particular kind of certainty has been tied to the work — the sketches, the timing, the way the whole system was supposed to be revealed.

I know it sounds extreme when I say it plainly, but I became very sure that a couple of clients, and even one editor, were trying to get access to my sketches before I was ready to unveil everything. It didn’t feel like normal worry, like “Oh, maybe they’re impatient,” or “Maybe they don’t understand my process.” It felt more definite than that, like there was a reason underneath what they were saying.

And they did reassure me. They told me it was just progress updates, scheduling, normal professional stuff. But it didn’t really settle me. I could hear the words, but I kept feeling like they wanted to see the structure before it was ready. So, no, I wouldn’t say it happens broadly across my whole life — it’s been centered on the work.
Has this worry about your work and sketches been causing you significant distress or interfering with your ability to function in your daily life?

Yes. I mean… I don’t like admitting that, because part of me still wants to say I’m just being careful with the work, that I’m protecting it. But yes, it has interfered.

My illustration deadlines have slipped, and not just by a little “artist being fussy” kind of way. I’ve gotten stuck trying to make sure the sketches weren’t seen too early or handled the wrong way, and then I lose days rechecking things, rearranging, holding back files, deciding whether it’s safe to send something. So the actual work doesn’t move forward the way it’s supposed to.

A couple of colleagues have had to check in on me, which was embarrassing. They were trying to be kind, I think, but it made me feel watched, and also ashamed because I know I’m usually more reliable than this. I’ve built my whole life around being able to deliver work.

And financially… that’s probably the part I’ve been avoiding saying out loud. I overcommitted myself and spent money I really needed to keep the studio secure. I thought I was setting things up properly, protecting the work, preparing for how it all needed to be presented. But now the mortgage is at risk, and that’s frightening. So yes, it’s not just in my head or just a private worry. It’s affected my work, my colleagues, and my ability to keep things stable.
Have you noticed any significant problems in your relationships with others, such as friends or family, due to your worries about work?

With friends and family… I’d say it’s less direct than with work people, if that makes sense. It hasn’t been like I’m constantly fighting with them about the sketches. But it has still affected things, because I’ve been so wrapped up in protecting the work and trying to keep the studio stable that I haven’t been as present.

The bigger problems have been around work itself. My illustration deadlines have slipped, and that creates this whole ripple effect where colleagues have had to check in on me, which I find humiliating, honestly. I know they’re probably just trying to make sure I’m okay or that the projects are moving, but it makes me feel exposed, like I’ve lost control of something I’m usually very careful with.

And then there’s the money side, which does affect the household, even if I try not to talk about it too much. I overcommitted myself and spent money I needed to keep the studio secure, because at the time I thought I was doing the responsible thing, preparing everything properly. But now the mortgage is at risk, and that’s… that’s hard to hide from people close to me. So yes, I suppose it has strained things, mostly because the work situation has started spilling into practical life.
Do you feel compelled to repeat certain behaviors over and over to reduce your anxiety?

I’m not sure I’d call it “compelled” in the way you mean. I don’t think I have a set ritual, exactly, like I have to do something a certain number of times or in a particular order or something like that.

I do sometimes go back over things more than I probably need to, especially with the work — checking what I’ve sent, what I haven’t sent, whether something is attached, whether someone can see a file before I meant them to. But I’m not sure if that’s what you’re asking about. It doesn’t feel like a separate behavior I repeat to make anxiety go away so much as… I get stuck trying to be careful, and then I lose time.

So I suppose my answer is: not in a clear, ritual kind of way. I haven’t really noticed anything like that outside of the work situation.
Do you still believe those clients and the editor had ulterior motives, despite their reassurances?

Yes… I did. I mean, I know how that sounds when I say it plainly, like I’m accusing people of something without proof, but at the time it felt very real to me.

A couple of clients, and even one editor, kept saying they were only asking for normal progress updates or early materials so they could plan around the project. And they reassured me — more than once — that they weren’t trying to take anything or interfere with how I wanted to present it. But it didn’t really settle me. I kept coming back to the idea that they were trying to get access to the sketches before I unveiled the whole system properly.

It wasn’t just a passing suspicion, either. It became this certainty in my mind, like I could see a pattern in their emails or in the timing of what they asked for. Even when they were being polite, I would think, “No, this is exactly how someone would sound if they were trying to get in early.” So reassurance didn’t really land the way it probably should have. Part of me could hear them saying the right things, but another part of me felt convinced there was something underneath it.
Have you felt like your worries about work and protecting your sketches have significantly impacted your ability to function normally in your daily life or maintain your relationships?

Yes, it has. I wish I could say it’s just been worry in my head and I’ve still been managing everything normally, but that wouldn’t be true.

My illustration deadlines have slipped, which is very unlike me and has caused problems professionally. People I work with have had to check in on me more than they should have to, and I find that really embarrassing — like I’m suddenly being monitored or like I can’t be trusted to handle my own work. And I know some of that is practical, because if I’m late then they need to know what’s happening, but it still feels awful.

And outside of work, the financial part has become serious. I overcommitted myself and spent money I really needed, because I thought I was protecting the studio and keeping things secure. At the time it felt necessary, like I was being careful and responsible, but now the mortgage is at risk. So yes, it’s definitely affecting daily life and the people close to me, because it’s not just an idea anymore — it’s turned into missed deadlines, people worrying about me, and real consequences at home.
Is the kind of worry you experience about your work and sketches something that you also experience in other areas of your life, such as your health or personal relationships?

Not really in the same way, no. I mean, I worry about ordinary things like anyone does — health, family, whether I’ve said the wrong thing to someone — but this particular kind of worry has been almost entirely tied to my work and the sketches.

It wasn’t like I was suspicious of everyone in every part of my life. It was more specific than that. I know it sounds extreme, and saying it now makes me feel a bit exposed, but I became really certain that a couple of clients, and even one editor, were trying to get access to the sketches before I unveiled the whole system properly. And the difficult part is that they did reassure me. They told me they just needed normal updates or materials for planning, and I could hear the words, but it didn’t settle me.

So, no, I wouldn’t say I have the same level of worry about my health or personal relationships. It’s been centered on protecting the work — like the sketches were vulnerable, and if I wasn’t careful, someone would get to them before I was ready.
Is the kind of excessive worry you experience about your work and sketches also something you experience in other areas of your life?

No, not in that same way. I mean, I do worry about other things, obviously, but this… this has been very specifically wrapped around the work and the sketches.

I know it sounds extreme when I say it out loud, and I don’t love admitting it, but I became really certain that a couple of clients — and even one editor — were trying to get access to my sketches before I unveiled the whole system properly. It felt like they were pushing for things too early, asking for materials or updates in a way that seemed normal on the surface, but to me it felt like there was something underneath it.

And they did reassure me. That’s the part that makes me feel a bit foolish now, because they weren’t being openly threatening or anything. They said they just needed the materials for ordinary planning reasons, but no amount of reassurance really settled me. I would hear what they were saying, and then my mind would sort of reinterpret it as, “Well, of course they’d say that if they were trying to get in before I was ready.” So it wasn’t really happening across every part of my life — it was centered on protecting the sketches.

target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds extreme, but I became certain a couple of clients and even one editor were trying to get access to my sketches before I unveiled the system, and no amount of reassurance from them really settled me.
target_item.reason: The question is asking about persistent irrational or unreasonable thoughts, which most closely matches the fixed suspicious belief that clients and an editor were trying to access the sketches despite reassurance.

patient.answer:
Yes… though I keep hesitating over the word “irrational,” because at the time it didn’t feel irrational. It felt like I was seeing something other people weren’t taking seriously enough.

The main thing was with my sketches. I became really convinced that a couple of clients, and even an editor I’ve worked with, were trying to get access to them before I was ready to unveil the larger system I’d been developing. Like when they asked for updates or wanted files, I didn’t hear it as just normal project management. I kept thinking, “No, they’re trying to get the framework before it’s complete,” or “They want to see the underlying structure so they can use it before I present it properly.”

And people did reassure me. They would say, “We’re not trying to take anything, we just need to see where the work is,” or “This is just for scheduling.” But it didn’t settle in. I could hear the words, and a part of me could understand that maybe it sounded extreme, but the certainty stayed there anyway. It was hard to let go of, even when I tried to talk myself down.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's thoughts are intrusive
doctor.question: Do you feel like these worries about your clients and editor are thoughts that pop into your head without you wanting them to?

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I know it sounds extreme, but I became certain a couple of clients and even one editor were trying to get access to my sketches before I unveiled the system, and no amount of reassurance from them really settled me.

patient.answer:
Not exactly like they “pop in” out of nowhere, no. It wasn’t like a random unwanted thought flashing through my mind and then I’d think, “Why am I thinking that?” It felt more… connected to what was happening. Like they would email asking for an update, or someone would mention needing to see the sketches, and then this whole certainty would come over me that they were trying to get access before I was ready to unveil the full system.

I know that probably sounds extreme, and I can hear that. But at the time it didn’t feel like just a nervous thought I could dismiss. It felt solid. I was certain a couple of clients, and even one editor, had some motive beyond what they were saying. And even when they reassured me — like, “No, we just need to see the progress,” or “This is normal scheduling stuff” — it didn’t really calm me down. I heard them, but it didn’t settle the feeling.

So… I wouldn’t say I wanted to be thinking about it, because it was stressful and made everything harder. But it also didn’t feel like some intrusive nonsense thought. It felt real, like I had to protect the sketches until I could reveal everything properly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's excessive worry is causing significant distress or impairment in their daily life
doctor.question: Has this worry about your work and sketches been causing you significant distress or interfering with your ability to function in your daily life?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: My illustration deadlines have slipped, colleagues have had to check in on me, and the mortgage is now at risk because I overcommitted and spent money I needed to keep the studio secure.
target_item.reason: The question directly asks whether the worry is causing significant distress or interfering with daily functioning, which corresponds to the functional impairment item.

patient.answer:
Yes. I mean… I don’t like admitting that, because part of me still wants to say I’m just being careful with the work, that I’m protecting it. But yes, it has interfered.

My illustration deadlines have slipped, and not just by a little “artist being fussy” kind of way. I’ve gotten stuck trying to make sure the sketches weren’t seen too early or handled the wrong way, and then I lose days rechecking things, rearranging, holding back files, deciding whether it’s safe to send something. So the actual work doesn’t move forward the way it’s supposed to.

A couple of colleagues have had to check in on me, which was embarrassing. They were trying to be kind, I think, but it made me feel watched, and also ashamed because I know I’m usually more reliable than this. I’ve built my whole life around being able to deliver work.

And financially… that’s probably the part I’ve been avoiding saying out loud. I overcommitted myself and spent money I really needed to keep the studio secure. I thought I was setting things up properly, protecting the work, preparing for how it all needed to be presented. But now the mortgage is at risk, and that’s frightening. So yes, it’s not just in my head or just a private worry. It’s affected my work, my colleagues, and my ability to keep things stable.

With friends and family… I’d say it’s less direct than with work people, if that makes sense. It hasn’t been like I’m constantly fighting with them about the sketches. The bigger problems have been around work itself. My illustration deadlines have slipped, and that creates this whole ripple effect where colleagues have had to check in on me, which I find humiliating, honestly. I know they’re probably just trying to make sure I’m okay or that the projects are moving, but it makes me feel exposed, like I’ve lost control of something I’m usually very careful with.

And then there’s the money side, which does affect the household, even if I try not to talk about it too much. I overcommitted myself and spent money I needed to keep the studio secure, because at the time I thought I was doing the responsible thing, preparing everything properly. But now the mortgage is at risk, and that’s… that’s hard to hide from people close to me. So yes, I suppose it has strained things, mostly because the work situation has started spilling into practical life.
